What the age of Olympia Fields houses means for lead paint

The honest answer for a 1970s-era house in Olympia Fields is probably yes, there is older paint under there, and paint that old can contain lead. What follows from that is method, not a refusal: sheeting, sealed doorways, dust kept where it is made, and a cleanup Olympia Fields homeowners should expect to see done properly.

In practice the rule is about containment and cleanup rather than about paint. In an Olympia Fields room it sets a threshold of roughly six square feet of disturbed interior paint, twenty square feet outside, and any window replacement or demolition is covered whatever the area. Sanding the casing on one 1979-median window clears that in a few minutes.

None of it is graded at the town line. The rule attaches to a build year and to the work being done, so the number worth checking is the one on your own deed in Olympia Fields.

The Census publishes a pre-1980 bucket rather than a pre-1978 one, and on that measure 51 percent of the housing sits on the older side of the line in Olympia Fields. Housing that old falls under the federal Renovation, Repair and Painting rule, which covers any work disturbing paint in a home built before 1978. Illinois is not an authorized state for it, so EPA runs it here directly.

The useful question is not whether the rule applies to your Olympia Fields house. At 36.1 percent pre-1970 it very likely does. The useful question is what the containment and the cleanup are actually going to look like in your rooms, and it is a fair one to ask anybody.

This site does not claim EPA lead-safe firm certification. No number has been supplied, so the trust panel below shows it as pending. Ask for it directly, from anyone quoting work in Olympia Fields.

Questions

Asked about Olympia Fields

Can it be done a room at a time?

Yes, and on 7.7-room housing it is often the right call. Doing one room properly beats doing four at a pace that shows, and it spreads the cost across seasons rather than across a credit card. Say that is what you want when you call, because it changes how the work is sequenced.

What changes the price most on a house here?

The state of the trim and the ceilings. Wall area is predictable, and with 7.7 median rooms and a 1979 median build year in Olympia Fields the woodwork is where the hours actually go. Ask for it as its own line and the differences between two quotes stop being mysterious.

Most of Olympia Fields is owner occupied. Does that change anything?

It changes what the work usually is. At 85.9 percent owner occupied, with 1,559 owner households, there is very little turnover painting here and a lot of repeat maintenance: exteriors on a cycle, one room at a time inside, trim and doors when they finally go. A maintained house and a neglected one are different jobs and should be different numbers, in both directions.

How is an interior price worked out for a house this size?

By trim, mostly. The median home in Olympia Fields runs 7.7 rooms, and rooms bring door casing, window casing and baseboard with them. Wall area is the fast part of an interior job and trim is the slow part, so a quote that gives one number for the whole house is hiding the half of it that actually varies. Ask for the trim separately.
